The Huichol, who call themselves Wixáritari, are an Indigenous people of the Sierra Madre Occidental in western Mexico, in the mountains of Jalisco, Nayarit, Zacatecas and Durango. Their language belongs to the Uto-Aztecan family and is close to that of the Cora.

Their rugged country kept the Spanish out for two centuries; the mountains of Nayarit were conquered only in 1722, and missions had little hold. The Huichol kept much of their old religion. Each year pilgrims walk hundreds of kilometres east to Wirikuta, a sacred desert in San Luis Potosí, to gather peyote, which they treat as a deity alongside the deer and maize.

They are known for yarn paintings and bead art showing their visions. Today about fifty thousand speak the language, and they defend Wirikuta against mining.
